title: The Secret Night Bakers
hook: Somebody is secretly baking Mr Pask's bread at night. Ivy is going to find out who.
blurb: Ivy has always wanted a real mystery, and now she has one. Mr Pask downstairs is eighty-one, his hands shake, and his bakery was about to close. But for two weeks his bread has been perfect. There are tiny footprints on the back step, missing dried apples, a bakery cat who won't go into the kitchen, and something small and prickly caught in the doormat. Ivy's casebook is ready. But solving the mystery turns out to be the easy part. Deciding what to do next is much harder.
coverAlt: Ivy peeping round a kitchen door at night with her notebook, discovering five hedgehogs making bread on a floury bakery table in the moonlight

narrator.notes: Lively, clever storytelling with dry humour in Ivy's casebook asides. Bramble is brisk, kind and no-nonsense. Mr Pask warm, slow and amused. From page 8 everything softens; the last page slow, quiet and drowsy.

style: Premium contemporary picture-book illustration for older readers: soft painterly 3D look, expressive characters, warm lamp-light and oven-glow against deep blue night, gentle film grain, detailed but uncluttered compositions with a little more realism and atmosphere than for younger books, cinematic depth of field. Consistent characters on every page. Absolutely no text, letters, numbers, signs or captions anywhere in the image; notebooks, clocks, flour bags and shop signs are always blank or turned away.
world: Pask's Bakery, a small old-fashioned corner bakery on a quiet British high street called Crumble Street, with a bay shop window, a striped awning and a green front door. Ivy's family lives in the flat above, reached by a narrow back staircase that comes down into the bakery kitchen. The kitchen: a big black cast-iron bread oven, a long scrubbed wooden table dusted with flour, sacks of flour, big ceramic mixing bowls, wooden spoons, tea towels, a high shelf of jars, a small window, and a back door with a cat flap that opens onto a tiny yard with a hawthorn hedge.

pages.heading: A Real Mystery
pages.text:
Ivy had always wanted a real mystery.

She had a notebook for it, with "Ivy's Casebook" on the cover. Inside were all her cases so far. The Missing Left Shoe (found in the fridge). The Strange Noise in the Bathroom (Dad, singing). Not one of them had been a real mystery.

Ivy lived in the flat above Pask's Bakery, on Crumble Street. Mr Pask had been baking bread there for sixty years. He was eighty-one now, and lately his hands shook. His loaves had come out flat and lumpy, and fewer people came in. Last month he had said, very quietly, that he might have to close.

Then, two weeks ago, something strange happened.

The bread was perfect again. Better than perfect. Golden crusts, soft middles, and a sweet, appley smell that made people stop in the street.

"Got my knack back," said Mr Pask, and winked.

Ivy didn't believe him for a second.
pages.imageAlt: Ivy in Pask's Bakery holding her notebook, eyeing Mr Pask suspiciously as he winks at her over a tray of perfect golden loaves

art.shot: Inside the shop, across the counter, early evening.
art.prompt: Inside the cosy old bakery shop at closing time, Mr Pask stands behind the wooden counter holding a tray of perfect golden loaves, giving a sly wink. Ivy stands on the customer side with her small red notebook open and pencil raised, one eyebrow lifted in deep suspicion. Shelves of bread behind him, a bay window with a blue evening street beyond. Warm, funny, intriguing.

pages.heading: Clues
pages.text:
Ivy turned to a fresh page and wrote CLUES at the top.

Clue one. Every morning there were tiny floury footprints on the back step. Each one had five little toes. They led across the yard and vanished under the hedge.

Clue two. Every night, a bag of dried apples went missing from the shelf by the oven.

Clue three. Duchess, the bakery cat, used to sleep in the warm kitchen. Now she wouldn't go near it after dark. She sat on the stairs instead, and glared.

Clue four was the strangest of all. Caught in the doormat was something small, stiff and sharp, striped brown and cream like a very thin pencil.

Ivy held it up to the light and frowned.

Whoever was baking Mr Pask's bread was very small, needed apples, and was, in some way she didn't yet understand, a bit prickly.

This was it. A real mystery, at last.
pages.imageAlt: Ivy crouched on the back step with a magnifying glass, studying tiny floury footprints, while Duchess the cat glares from the doorway

art.shot: Low angle on the back step, Ivy crouched close to the ground.
art.prompt: Ivy crouches on the bakery's back step in the morning light with a magnifying glass, studying a trail of tiny floury footprints with five little toes leading across the small yard towards a hawthorn hedge. In her other hand she holds up a single thin striped spine between finger and thumb. Duchess, the large fluffy grey cat, sits in the open back doorway glaring disapprovingly. Curious, clever, atmospheric.

pages.heading: Suspects
pages.text:
Next, Ivy made a list of suspects.

Suspect one: Duchess. Crossed out at once. Duchess could not reach the oven, and anyway, she was clearly frightened of something.

Suspect two: the night bus driver, who bought a bun every morning at five o'clock. But when Ivy asked him about it at the bus stop, he sneezed so hard his hat fell off. "Flour," he sniffed. "Can't go near the stuff." Crossed out.

Suspect three was just a question mark.

Ivy chewed her pencil. There was only one way to find out. She would have to see it with her own eyes.

On Friday night she packed her stakeout bag: casebook, pencil, torch, a cushion for the stairs, and two custard creams, for energy.

Then she lay in bed with her cardigan on and waited for Mum and Dad to fall asleep.
pages.imageAlt: Ivy in bed with her cardigan on, wide awake, her stakeout bag packed beside her and Duchess at the foot of the bed

art.shot: Medium view of Ivy's small bedroom at night.
art.prompt: Ivy lies in bed in her pyjamas with her mustard cardigan on over the top, covers pulled up, eyes wide open and determined, staring at the ceiling. Beside the bed sits a small packed canvas bag with a torch, a cushion and her red notebook poking out, and two rectangular cream-filled biscuits on top. A pinboard on the wall shows a few blank cards joined by red string, detective-style. Duchess the grey cat sleeps at the foot of the bed. Funny and full of anticipation, lamp just switched off, moonlight at the window.

pages.heading: The Stakeout
pages.text:
At midnight, Ivy crept down the back stairs that led from the flat to the bakery kitchen. She put her cushion on the third step from the bottom, where she could see through the gap in the door.

The kitchen was dark and still. The big oven ticked as it cooled. Ivy waited. And waited.

She ate one custard cream, for energy. Then the other one, for more energy.

Her eyes began to droop. She was just deciding that being a detective was mostly waiting, when she heard it.

Pitter-patter. Pitter-patter.

Ivy's eyes snapped open.

The cat flap in the back door swung. Something came through it. Then four more somethings, smaller and rounder, rolling in one after the other like conkers.

Ivy held her breath.
pages.imageAlt: Ivy on the dark back stairs peering through the gap in the kitchen door as small round shapes come through the cat flap

art.shot: Over Ivy's shoulder on the stairs, looking through the gap in the door.
art.prompt: Ivy sits on a cushion on the narrow dark back stairs, peering through the gap of a half-open door into the moonlit bakery kitchen, one hand over her mouth, eyes wide. Across the kitchen, the cat flap in the back door swings open and several small round spiky silhouettes are tumbling through it in a line, lit by moonlight from the small window. The big black oven glows faintly. Suspenseful but cosy, never frightening.

pages.heading: The Night Bakers
pages.text:
In the moonlight from the window, Ivy saw them clearly.

Hedgehogs. Five of them.

The biggest one had a tea towel tied round her middle like an apron. She clapped her small paws once, and the others got to work.

Two little hedgehogs pushed a bag of flour across the floor. One climbed onto another's back and tipped it into the big bowl. Another stirred with a wooden spoon held in both paws.

Then came the best part. They tipped the dough onto the table and climbed up after it. Then they kneaded it with their feet, marching up and down, up and down, like tiny soldiers.

Last of all, the biggest hedgehog reached for the bag of dried apples.

Ivy had to put both hands over her mouth so she wouldn't laugh.
pages.imageAlt: Five hedgehogs making bread on the floury kitchen table, the young ones marching on the dough while Bramble reaches for the dried apples

art.shot: At table height, the whole busy scene on the floury table.
art.prompt: On the long floury wooden table in the moonlit bakery kitchen, the four Hoglets march up and down on a big round lump of dough, kneading it with their feet like tiny soldiers, flour puffing up around them. Bramble, the plump old hedgehog in tiny spectacles and a checked tea-towel apron, stands at the edge of the table, reaching for a paper bag of dried apples. A big ceramic bowl and a wooden spoon lie nearby. Delightful, funny, full of wonder.

pages.heading: Caught
pages.text:
Then Ivy's slipper slipped off the step. Bump.

Five hedgehogs froze. The four small ones curled into tight, prickly balls and rolled under the table.

The biggest hedgehog didn't run. She walked right up to the door and looked at Ivy over a pair of tiny spectacles.

"Well," she said. "You'd better come in, then. Mind the dough."

Her name was Bramble. She sat on an upturned egg cup and told Ivy everything.

For forty years, Mr Pask had put out water and a saucer of cat biscuits for the hedgehogs under the hedge. Every single night. (Duchess had never forgiven him.)

"Now his hands shake," said Bramble. "And he was going to close. So we help. We make the dough at night, and he bakes it in the morning." She peered at Ivy. "But nobody must know. Hedgehogs are shy. And Mr Pask is proud."
pages.imageAlt: Ivy sitting on the kitchen floor listening to Bramble the hedgehog, who sits on an upturned egg cup, while small hedgehogs peep out from under the table

art.shot: Low, at floor level, Ivy cross-legged facing Bramble.
art.prompt: Ivy sits cross-legged on the moonlit kitchen floor in her cardigan and pyjamas, notebook on her knee, listening intently. Opposite her, Bramble the old hedgehog sits on an upturned egg cup, peering at Ivy over her tiny spectacles and explaining with one raised paw. Behind them, under the table, the four Hoglets peep out from curled-up balls, curious. Warm, conspiratorial and gentle.

pages.heading: The Biggest Story on Crumble Street
pages.text:
Ivy looked down at her casebook.

This was the biggest mystery ever solved on Crumble Street. If she told, it would be in the newspaper. People would come from miles away to see the hedgehogs who baked bread. Ivy could almost hear the clapping.

Then she thought about what would really happen.

Crowds at the back door. Cameras in the hedge. Five shy hedgehogs gone by the next night, never to come back. And Mr Pask in his empty kitchen, with everyone saying it had never really been his bread at all.

Ivy closed the casebook. On the cover, under her name, she wrote two new words: Case Unsolved.

"I won't tell," she said. "Ever."

Bramble looked at her for a long moment. Then she nodded, once, the way you nod at a friend.

"In that case," she said, "you can do the apples."
pages.imageAlt: Ivy writing on the cover of her closed notebook while Bramble watches her thoughtfully

art.shot: Close view, Ivy's thoughtful face and the notebook, Bramble beside her.
art.prompt: Close view of Ivy sitting on the kitchen floor, her closed red notebook on her knee, pencil to its blank cover, her face serious and thoughtful as she makes up her mind. Bramble stands beside her knee, watching her with a long, wise, approving look. Soft moonlight from the window and the faint glow of the oven. Quiet, important, warm.

pages.heading: You Knew
pages.text:
Ivy did the apples, pressing them into the dough one by one. Then they covered it with a clean cloth to rise, the way all good bakers do. When it was resting, the hedgehogs rolled out through the cat flap: one, two, three, four, five. Then Ivy crept back up to bed.

She woke at five to the smell of baking, and tiptoed down in her slippers.

Mr Pask was lifting loaves out of the oven, golden and steaming. He did not look surprised to see her.

Ivy noticed three things. By the back door was a fresh saucer of water. On the table was a brand-new bag of dried apples. And under the table, where there had never been one before, stood a tiny wooden step, exactly the right height for a hedgehog.

"You knew," Ivy whispered. "All along."

Mr Pask smiled, and put one floury finger to his lips.
pages.imageAlt: Mr Pask lifting golden loaves from the oven at dawn, a finger to his lips, as Ivy realises he knew all along

art.shot: Medium view of the kitchen at dawn, Ivy at the foot of the stairs.
art.prompt: Early dawn light through the small kitchen window. Mr Pask, in his flour-dusted apron and baker's cap, holds a tray of golden steaming loaves fresh from the open oven and raises one floury finger to his lips with a warm, knowing smile. Ivy stands at the bottom of the back stairs in her cardigan and slippers, mouth open in realisation. A saucer of water sits by the back door, a paper bag on the table, and a tiny wooden step under the table. Warm, golden and heartfelt.

pages.heading: Kept Together
pages.text:
"Some secrets," said Mr Pask, "are best kept together."

He gave Ivy the first warm apple bun of the day and took the second for himself. They sat on the back step to eat while the sky went pink over the rooftops. Duchess sat between them, pretending she had never been frightened of anything in her life.

"They think I don't know," said Mr Pask. "And I think they'd stop if they knew I knew. So I keep quiet, they keep baking, and everyone's happy."

Ivy worked it out on her fingers. "So now I know that you know, but they don't know that you know."

Mr Pask laughed so much he had to hold on to the door frame.

"That," he said, wiping his eyes, "is exactly right."
pages.imageAlt: Ivy and Mr Pask sitting on the back step at sunrise eating warm apple buns, with Duchess between them

art.shot: From the yard, looking back at the step, sunrise behind the rooftops.
art.prompt: Ivy and Mr Pask sit side by side on the bakery's back step at sunrise, each holding a warm apple bun, Mr Pask laughing with his head back. Duchess the fluffy grey cat sits primly between them. The sky over the rooftops is soft pink and gold. The hawthorn hedge at the side of the yard has a tiny pointed nose peeping out from underneath it. Joyful, warm and calm.

pages.heading: Not Telling
pages.text:
That night, Ivy lay in bed and listened.

From down below came the faint pitter-patter of small feet, and the soft thump, thump, thump of dough being marched on. The smell of apples drifted up through the floorboards.

Ivy opened her casebook one last time. Under Clues and Suspects, she wrote a question: Who is baking Mr Pask's bread?

Then, underneath, very neatly: Not telling.

She slid the casebook under her pillow and switched off her torch.

Thump, thump, went the tiny feet downstairs.

Thump... thump...

Ivy was asleep long before the dough had finished rising.
pages.imageAlt: Ivy asleep in bed with her notebook under her pillow, the room dim and calm in the moonlight

art.shot: Soft close view of Ivy asleep, from beside the bed.
art.prompt: Ivy lies fast asleep in bed on her side, both hands tucked under her cheek, a small contented smile. Her red notebook is hidden UNDER her pillow: only one small red corner pokes out from beneath the pillow's edge; she is not holding it. Her torch lies on the bedside table, switched OFF: its lens is dark, giving no light at all. Faint warm light glows up through the gaps in the old wooden floorboards from the bakery kitchen below. Soft moonlight at the window. Very dim, soft, low-contrast, peaceful and cosy.
